b: I'm not quite the man I used to be.

I could work long, intense hours, whilst raising kids and still getting exercise and little sleep. Our family could live on a shoestring budget, with second hand furniture, cheap housing and used motor cars.
And we were pretty good at it. We managed to build careers, save and invest some money, and most importantly, turn some kids into pretty respectable young adults.
But it was hard. Really hard.

So when I watched a video from Heather Flynn, encouraging us to "do the hard things", I could understand where she was coming from. It builds character, improves health, relationships and finances. But doing the hard things is also .... hard. It takes energy and commitment that are not always abundant throughout our lives.

Which got me thinking about the financial arc we traverse throughout our lives. As young adults most of start with nothing, maybe less with nothing if we are carrying debt from tertiary education. We survive on minimal income, either because we are working part time while studying or starting at the very bottom rung of the career ladder. But we toil away, find ways to make our meagre income work.

If we are lucky we can create a gap between our income and our living expenses, and put some money to long term investments. And hopefully we can increase our income to ease the financial pressure, enjoy a few more luxuries, and boost those investments along a little.

We hope that eventually we reach a point where we look at our investments with some degree of pride and comfort. As our financial situation improves and the years chip away at our energy levels, doing the hard things doesn't seem to be so attractive any more.
So, in a grossly simplistic fashion, maybe all financial planning is "do the hard things now, so you don't have to later".
